Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?
Motivation: browse scrollback and copy with visual selection in one area while composing or quoting in another — analogous to two views of one buffer in vim (without shared-buffer semantics).
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?

Short answer: tmux does not offer a vim-style “one buffer, two views” for a single pane’s scrollback. Copy mode always occupies the whole pane you started it in, and it only shows that pane’s history. A split gives two independent PTYs with separate scrollback buffers, so a copy-mode browser in the top pane is not automatically the same stream as the shell in the bottom pane.
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?

What the “other” pane is doing: In a split layout, each pane is just another shell (or another program). There is no built-in “mirror this pane’s scrollback here” mode. The bottom can stay your normal shell; the top would only match that scrollback if you copy data over (see below), not because tmux links two views of one buffer.
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?

Split + copy mode in the pane that owns the history — If all the output you care about is in the bottom pane, enter copy mode there (Prefix+[). You lose simultaneous typing in that same pane until you exit copy mode, but you can yank to tmux’s buffer or the OS clipboard and then move focus to another pane to paste (Prefix+], or Cmd+V if your config bridges to the clipboard). That matches “select upstairs, use downstairs” across panes, but not two live views of one scrollback.
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?

Snapshot scrollback into the other pane — From the pane that has the history, push text out with capture-pane and read it in the second pane, e.g. tmux capture-pane -S -5000 -p -t 'session:window.pane' | less or into nvim. That is a point-in-time copy, not a continuously synced second view (re-run to refresh).
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?

Log the stream for a true second window — pipe-pane (or shell tee) can append live output to a file; a split can run less +F file / tail -f on that file. Good for forward-looking duplication; older scrollback before logging started is not magically shared.

synchronize-panes — Sends the same keystrokes to multiple panes; it does not tie scrollback together like scrollbind, and it is a poor fit for “browse in copy mode while typing elsewhere.” See discussion in this Stack Overflow thread.
Is it possible to split a tmux pane for copy-mode scrollback above and live shell below like vim?

Bottom line: The vim analogy breaks because a terminal pane is not a text buffer — it is a PTY with one display state. For “read old output while editing,” splitting in tmux helps spatially (reference + work side by side); bridging content is via yank/paste, capture-pane, or logging, not a native dual-view scrollback.

The piece that's missing is the session toggle: <prefix> L (capital L, default binding for switch-client -l) switches the client back to the last session it was attached to, including one you just left via the session picker.

Is there a keyshort to jump back to my previous window, even in a different session, after using tmux/Prefix w to open the tmux/session/Picker?
Is there a technical underpinning to bind this as one keyshort in a plugin?

For anything smarter than a fixed chain — e.g. only running last-window when the session actually changed, or tracking the exact previously active pane rather than tmux's own single last-session/last-window pointers — a plugin would use run-shell to call a script, and persist its own state between key presses with user options (set -g @my_var ..., read back via #{@my_var} or show-options -gv). The same .tmux.conf uses this exact user-option pattern (e.g. @battery_percentage, @battery_charge) to cache values across separate command invocations.

What does it mean to "zoom" a tmux pane, and how do you zoom out?

What “zoom” means: In tmux, zoom is a per-window layout toggle on the active pane. The pane is marked zoomed and temporarily expands to use the entire client area for that window; other panes in the same window stay in the layout but are not drawn until you leave zoomed state. Under the hood this is the resize-pane -Z behavior exposed as the default binding prefix + z (see tmux(1) — default key bindings).
What does it mean to "zoom" a tmux pane, and how do you zoom out?

How to zoom out: Press the same key again — prefix + z toggles zoom on and off for the current pane (same binding as zoom in). There is not a separate “zoom out” chord in the default table; it is one toggle.
What does it mean to "zoom" a tmux pane, and how do you zoom out?

Naming note: People coming from vim sometimes say <leader> z, but in tmux documentation and configs the chord is almost always written as <prefix> z where prefix is your prefix key (often Ctrl-b by default, or whatever you set with set -g prefix).

What expands every item in tmux tree mode, and why does Cmd-plus resize the Ghostty font instead?
What expands every item in tmux tree mode, and why does Cmd-plus resize the Ghostty font instead?

Short answer: tmux/Mode/Tree binds expand-all to M-+, and M- is Key/Meta — on that is ⌥, never ⌘. ⌘+ is Ghostty's own font-size binding and is swallowed before tmux can see it. Even the right keystroke only opens the tree as deep as it was built, so after tmux/Prefix w it does nothing. Opening the tree with choose-tree -Z shows sessions, windows, and panes at once.

What expands every item in tmux tree mode, and why does Cmd-plus resize the Ghostty font instead?

Key/Meta on macOS is ⌥, and only when the terminal is told to send it that way. macos-option-as-alt = true in the Ghostty config makes ⌥⇧= send ESC then +, which tmux reads as M-+. Ghostty ships no built-in alt+ binding for + or =, so nothing intercepts it on the way through — unlike alt+arrow_left and alt+arrow_right, which do collide (see tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Resize Pane).

Short answer: a -t target is parsed as session:window.pane, so a dot inside the session name is read as the window/pane separator. The lookup then runs against a window or a pane that does not exist, and the error names that window or pane rather than the session — which is why it reads as a missing session. Keep dots out of session names.

Short answer: The tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Resize Pane bindings are still calling resize-pane on the active pane. In a nested layout they only move the immediate vertical border between the two bottom panes. If that border cannot move—most often because the other bottom pane is already at tmux’s minimum width—the command no-ops, which looks like “resize doesn’t work.” Alt-Up / Alt-Down still move the outer (full-width) horizontal divider, where there is usually more slack in rows than you have spare columns in the bottom row, so those resizes are more likely to succeed.
